posts.title: Report: Inside the Horror of Saudi Arabia’s Kafala System
posts.description: Nearly two years after Faith Wambui boarded a plane out of Kenya, hoping to build a better life for herself and her son as a domestic worker abroad, she gave birth on a bed inside a brothel in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.The child was conceived after Wambui, now thirty-eight, was coerced into sex by her Saudi employer’s brother in exchange for food. She named him Bilal, after Bilal ibn Rabah, the African-born former slave who became one of the Prophet Muhammad’s most trusted companions.With the same razor used to cut the umbilical cord, Wambui carved the initials BW deep into the back of his shoulder. She had seen other women do the same.“There were so many women giving birth to half-Arab babies who all looked similar; we were worried our children would get mixed up,” Wambui tells me outside a building on Nairobi’s outskirts, left open by its owner to people living on the streets. posts.title: German Christian-Democrats Go Cold on LGBTQ Rights
posts.description: Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel, who has occasionally reflected publicly on her political legacy, recently acknowledged another mistake from her sixteen-year tenure. If she could decide again on the issue of marriage equality, she told the Kaffee und Fluchen podcast on November 13, “I would vote for it today, yes.” At the time, she had various concerns, particularly regarding surrogacy and children. She had already taken a self-critical look at her no vote in her memoir, titled Freedom.On June 30, 2017, the Bundestag voted 393 to 226 to expand marriage rights to same-sex couples. The majority ultimately reflected the reality in German society: In an Insa poll conducted for right-wing paper Bild the day before the vote, just under 75 percent of respondents supported marriage equality, while only about 20 percent opposed it. posts.title: In Europe, Too, Amazon’s Warehouses Are a Dystopia
posts.description: When you see it, it’s hard to believe that nobody, at any point from planning to installation, raised a hand to say how tone-deaf it was. But there it is, emblazoned in bright colors above the gates where workers enter an Amazon warehouse in Germany:“Work hard. Have fun. Make history.”The corporate Americana and hyperoptimistic bravado are enough to make us wince. In Germany, of all places, words about work above an iron gate also bring to mind a much darker time and another slogan about work and freedom. It’s a terrible look.That gate was our introduction to a fact-finding mission to Amazon warehouses in Germany and Poland. On October 26 and 27, we joined a delegation from the European Parliament’s Committee on Employment and Social Affairs at the company’s sites in Mönchengladbach, Dortmund, and Sosnowiec, near Katowice.The visit was long overdue.
